claims.text: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed primarily by the stability and integrity of a protective oxide layer formed during sliding.
Protective oxide-layer stability in FeNiCrCoCu coatings depends on alloy composition and microstructure.
Changing the FeNiCrCoCu coating from nanocrystalline to microcrystalline will increase oxide-layer continuity and adherence.
Increasing the coating grain size will improve high-temperature wear resistance.
Post-deposition annealing can increase the FeNiCrCoCu coating grain size from nanocrystalline to microcrystalline.
Larger grains reduce grain-boundary diffusion in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Reduced grain-boundary diffusion promotes formation of a more continuous and adherent oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
A continuous and adherent oxide layer acts as a barrier against further wear.
Microcrystalline FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have lower wear rates than nanocrystalline coatings under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
Microcrystalline FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have more stable friction coefficients than nanocrystalline coatings under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The predicted reduction in wear and stabilization of friction are caused by improved oxide-layer integrity.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to FeNiCrCoCu thin films on conventional metal substrates at temperatures above 500°C and under moderate-to-high sliding loads.
Oxide-layer formation is assumed to dominate wear resistance within the stated high-temperature regime.
Failure of the microcrystalline coating to show lower wear rates and more stable friction, or failure to improve oxide-layer integrity, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The test range includes 500°C, whereas the stated applicability boundary is temperatures above 500°C, leaving applicability at exactly 500°C inconsistent.
